questions.prompt: Why does the title "The Big C" matter after Chapter 6?
choices: It is the strongest on-disk place for the remaining C force after E.D.S.O.
It proves the book has abandoned the chemical frame
It means the chapter is mainly about accounting

explanation.gentle: The sequencing matters. Chapter 6 grouped four named forces, so this title is the logical place for the remaining C force.
explanation.direct: After E.D.S.O., The Big C is the clearest on-disk chapter for isolating the remaining fifth pressure.
explanation.competitive: Four got grouped first so one big force could step out alone here.

questions.prompt: What is the safest practical way to teach Chapter 7?
choices: As chronic alarm or threat pressure that keeps a room braced
As a complete medical explanation of one chemical
As a chapter with no leadership application

explanation.gentle: The source freeze is thin, so the safest lesson is the lived force of chronic alarm rather than a technical lecture.
explanation.direct: The chapter works best when taught as threat pressure that distorts culture over time.
explanation.competitive: You do not need lab detail to understand a room that forgot how to exhale.

questions.prompt: What usually happens first in a chronically braced room?
choices: People relax more deeply into trust
People become more guarded and edit what they reveal
People stop caring about work entirely

explanation.gentle: Fear pressure does not usually remove effort first. It makes people protect themselves first.
explanation.direct: The early shift is toward guardedness, later truth, and narrower cooperation.
explanation.competitive: Alarm trains cover before it kills motion.

questions.prompt: Rina's team gets frequent late-night "urgent" emails and starts hiding delays until they have a clean story. What does Chapter 7 say is going on?
choices: The team lacks ambition
The environment is teaching chronic alarm, so exposure feels costly
Late-night work is always healthy for high performers

explanation.gentle: This is a chronic-threat pattern: the room learns that honesty is risky, so people edit first.
explanation.direct: The system is making the body expect the next hit, which bends truth toward self-protection.
explanation.competitive: The alarm is in charge now, and the team is learning to survive it instead of speak through it.

questions.prompt: Why can a fearful room still look efficient for a while?
choices: Because fear often preserves visible motion even while it weakens trust
Because trust is irrelevant to performance
Because fear automatically creates wisdom

explanation.gentle: The trap is that fear can keep people moving before its deeper cost becomes obvious.
explanation.direct: Threat can preserve punctual behavior while degrading honesty and cooperation underneath.
explanation.competitive: Fear can fake strength long enough to fool a leader.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between real pressure and normalized threat in this chapter?
choices: Real pressure disappears forever, while threat never does
Real pressure can coexist with protection, while normalized threat keeps the room braced all the time
There is no meaningful difference

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps room for standards and urgency. The problem begins when people never get to stand down safely.
explanation.direct: A demanding room still contains predictability and protection; a threatening room makes alarm permanent.
explanation.competitive: Pressure tests people. Threat trains them to live in defense.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 7 fit the book's contrast between trust and paranoia so well?
choices: Because chronic alarm can make paranoia and self-interest adaptive
Because trust and paranoia are only personality traits
Because the chapter rejects all team structure

explanation.gentle: The chapter explains how a fearful environment can push people toward guarded, self-protective behavior.
explanation.direct: Paranoia and self-interest often grow as adaptation to threat, not just as personal ideology.
explanation.competitive: A braced room does not need a selfish philosophy when fear already makes selfishness look prudent.

questions.prompt: What limit must the chapter preserve to stay useful?
choices: That all demanding environments are harmful
That standards and deadlines are real, but leaders must stop them from becoming permanent alarm
That only calm environments can produce good work

explanation.gentle: The chapter is not anti-standards. It is against turning pressure into a constant fearful atmosphere.
explanation.direct: Real accountability matters; the failure begins when leaders normalize alarm instead of containing it.
explanation.competitive: Toughness is not the same thing as keeping the room in fight-or-flight all day.

questions.prompt: What does Chapter 7 imply about values slogans in a fearful culture?
choices: They can help, but they do not defeat chronic threat by themselves
They automatically remove fear
They are irrelevant because culture cannot change

explanation.gentle: Fear is environmental, so slogans alone cannot fix the force if the room stays braced.
explanation.direct: Values language does not beat alarm unless the system also changes what makes people feel exposed.
explanation.competitive: Posters lose to panic if the panic keeps paying better.

questions.prompt: If The Big C names chronic alarm, what kind of later leadership response becomes necessary?
choices: Leaders who absorb pressure instead of spreading it through the room
Leaders who create even more uncertainty
Leaders who ignore fear and focus only on output

explanation.gentle: Later courage and leadership chapters would need people willing to protect others from spreading threat.
explanation.direct: Once fear is named as a culture force, leadership must mean containing pressure rather than amplifying it.
explanation.competitive: If alarm is the enemy, the next real leader is the one who takes the hit instead of spraying it outward.
